keep: Merit over bloodline was a weapon before it was a value.
lede: An outcast boy on the steppe who survived captivity and near-starvation, and forged the largest contiguous land empire in history.
copy: Born Temüjin, he united the warring nomadic tribes and built an empire stretching, at its height, from Korea to Hungary. The conquests were staggeringly violent; whole cities were erased. Yet to reduce him to a destroyer is to miss why historians keep returning to him.

He ran a meritocracy in an age of bloodlines, promoting commanders on ability rather than birth. He established a written Mongol script, guaranteed religious freedom across his domains, abolished torture as policy in places, protected diplomats and merchants, and stitched together a Eurasian trade and communication network — the Pax Mongolica — along which goods, technologies and ideas (paper, printing, gunpowder, the compass) flowed west and reshaped the world.
More than the borders he drew, it is this circulation of knowledge, and the genetic and cultural fingerprint he left across a continent, that makes the case for him as a maker of the modern world.

bio.t: Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World
bio.why: Drawing on the long-suppressed Secret History of the Mongols and years of fieldwork, Weatherford overturns the cartoon villain and argues for Genghis Khan as an unlikely modernizer.

contested: This is the most disputed pick on the shelf. Weatherford's revisionism is vivid and hugely influential in the popular view, but Mongol-studies specialists have criticised it as over-corrective, thin on some sources and prone to crediting the Mongols with developments that predate or postdate them. Read it against Timothy May or Christopher Atwood for the scholarly account.
